content.text:
**Fix the part-number matching now, and skip the pre-change survey.**

**Why:**
- The evidence is already strong and behavioural, which beats stated opinion. 18% of searches return nothing, the top zero-result terms are mostly part numbers that differ only by dashes or spaces, and sales logs about 340 "can't find part" calls a month. These three sources agree on the cause.
- A satisfaction survey would measure sentiment. It wouldn't tell you why searches fail. It would also take weeks and get a low response rate, and it would delay a fix that takes three days.
- The change is cheap and easy to reverse. Normalising punctuation and case in part-number matching has little downside, and you can roll it back.

**How to keep the head of sales onside:**
- Treat their instinct as a measurement need. Record the baseline now: zero-result rate, calls tagged "can't find part online", and search-to-order conversion.
- Ship the fix, then compare after 2–4 weeks. Expect the zero-result rate and the tagged calls to fall. This is a better test than a survey, because it uses real behaviour.
- If you want customer voice, run a short survey or a few calls after the fix, aimed at the searches that still fail.

**Caveats:**
- Normalisation won't fix every zero-result term. Some will be parts you don't stock, superseded numbers, or descriptive queries. Check the remaining top terms after launch.
- I haven't seen the logs, so the "most of the top 200" claim and the cause of the 340 calls rest on your summary. A quick look at a sample of the tagged calls would confirm that part numbers are the cause.

**Next steps:** Approve the three days, capture the baseline this week, and review the results in a month.
